content.prompt: Determine whether the following are geometric sequences.

answer.worked: $$\frac{6}{2}=\frac{18}{6}=\frac{54}{18}=\frac{162}{54}=3.$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=3$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{-2}{1}&=\frac{4}{-2}=\frac{-8}{4}=-2\\\frac{16}{-8}&=\frac{-32}{16}=-2.\end{aligned}$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=-2$.
$$\frac{5}{2}\ne\frac{10}{5}=2.$$The consecutive-term ratios are not constant, so the sequence is not geometric.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2}&=\sqrt{2}\\\frac{4}{2\sqrt{2}}&=\sqrt{2}\\\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{4}&=\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=\sqrt{2}$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\div\frac{1}{2}&=\frac{1}{5}\times2=\frac{2}{5}\\\frac{2}{25}\div\frac{1}{5}&=\frac{2}{25}\times5=\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=\frac{2}{5}$.

content.prompt:
Find the ratios $\dfrac{a_2}{a_1}$ and $\dfrac{a_3}{a_2}$ for each sequence to test whether it is a GP.

If the sequence is a GP, write down the first term $a$ and the common ratio $r$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{8}{4}=2\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{16}{8}=2\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=4$ and $r=2$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{8}{16}=\frac12\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{4}{8}=\frac12\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=16$ and $r=\frac12$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{4}{2}=2\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{6}{4}=\frac32\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are different, so it is not a GP.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{-100}{-1000}=\frac1{10}\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{-10}{-100}=\frac1{10}\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=-1000$ and $r=\frac1{10}$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{40}{-80}=-\frac12\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{-20}{40}=-\frac12\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=-80$ and $r=-\frac12$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{29}{29}=1\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{29}{29}=1\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=29$ and $r=1$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{4}{1}=4\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are different, so it is not a GP.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{14}{-14}=-1\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{-14}{14}=-1\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=-14$ and $r=-1$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{1}{6}\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{\frac16}{1}=\frac16\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=6$ and $r=\frac16$.

content.prompt: A piece of paper $0.1$ mm thick is folded successively $100$ times. How thick is it now? Give an exact answer in millimetres and an approximation in kilometres to 3 significant figures.

answer.worked:
Each fold doubles the thickness. Including the initial thickness, the geometric sequence has $a=0.1$, $r=2$ and $101$ terms.
$$\begin{align*}a_{101}&=ar^{100}\\a_{101}&=0.1\times2^{100}\\a_{101}&=\frac{2^{100}}{10}\text{ mm}.\end{align*}$$
Since $1\text{ km}=10^6\text{ mm}$, the thickness is
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2^{100}}{10\times10^6}\text{ km}&=\frac{2^{100}}{10^7}\text{ km}\\&\approx1.27\times10^{23}\text{ km}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A principal $P$ dollars is invested at 7% per annum compound interest. Let $A_n$ be the total amount at the end of $n$ years.

answer.worked:
The first term is $a=1.07P$ and the common ratio is $r=1.07$.
$$\begin{align*}A_n&=ar^{n-1}\\A_n&=(1.07P)(1.07)^{n-1}\\A_n&=P(1.07)^n\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use trial-and-error on the calculator to find how many full years it will take for the amount to double, and how many years it will take for it to exceed ten times the original principal.

answer.short: 11 years to double; 35 years to exceed ten times the original principal.
answer.worked:
To double, require $A_n\ge2P$, so $(1.07)^n\ge2$. Calculator trials give
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^{10}&\approx1.9672<2\\(1.07)^{11}&\approx2.1049>2\end{align*}$$
The first full year is 11.

To exceed ten times the principal, require $A_n>10P$, so $(1.07)^n>10$. Calculator trials give
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^{34}&\approx9.9781<10\\(1.07)^{35}&\approx10.6766>10\end{align*}$$
The first full year is 35.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Use logarithms to confirm your answer.

answer.short: Doubling requires $n\ge\log_{1.07}2\approx10.24$, giving 11 years. Exceeding ten times the principal requires $n>\log_{1.07}10\approx34.03$, giving 35 years.
answer.worked:
For doubling:
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^n&\ge2\\n&\ge\log_{1.07}2\\\log_{1.07}2&\approx10.24\end{align*}$$
The least whole number of years is 11.

For exceeding ten times the principal:
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^n&>10\\n&>\log_{1.07}10\\\log_{1.07}10&\approx34.03\end{align*}$$
The least whole number of years is 35.

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned}20000(0.8)^n&<2000\\(0.8)^n&<0.1\end{aligned}$

By trial and error:

$\begin{aligned}W_{10}&=20000(0.8)^{10}\approx\$2147.48\\W_{11}&=20000(0.8)^{11}\approx\$1717.99\end{aligned}$

The value first falls below $\$2000$ after 11 complete years.

The inequality reverses because the logarithm has base $0.8$, between 0 and 1. The least whole number satisfying this is $n=11$, so it takes 11 complete years.

content.prompt: Find the $n$th term of each GP in fully simplified form.

answer.worked:

inlines.text: Consider the infinite geometric series below:
Try adding the first 10 terms of this series. What do you notice about the partial sums?

answer.short: The first ten partial sums are $1,3,7,15,31,63,127,255,511,1023$. They increase without bound.
answer.worked:
Adding successive terms gives $1,3,7,15,31,63,127,255,511,1023$.
$$\begin{align*}S_n&=\frac{1(1-2^n)}{1-2}\\S_n&=2^n-1\end{align*}$$
As $n\to\infty$, the partial sums increase without bound, so there is no limiting sum.

inlines.text: Try adding the first 10 terms of this series using a calculator. What do you notice?

answer.short: $S_{10}=1.998046875$. The partial sums approach 2 from below.
answer.worked:
The first ten partial sums are $1$, $1.5$, $1.75$, $1.875$, $1.9375$, $1.96875$, $1.984375$, $1.9921875$, $1.99609375$, $1.998046875$.
$$\begin{align*}S_n&=\frac{1-(\frac12)^n}{1-\frac12}\\S_n&=2\left(1-\left(\frac12\right)^n\right)\end{align*}$$
As $n\to\infty$, $(\frac12)^n\to0$, so the partial sums approach 2 from below.

inlines.text: For some geometric series, there is a
Investigate what happens to the partial sum of a geometric series when:
For a positive first term, partial sums increase without bound.
For a positive first term, partial sums increase towards a finite limit.
Partial sums alternate about a finite limit, getting closer to it.
Partial sums oscillate with increasing magnitude; there is no limiting sum.

answer.worked: For a non-zero first term, use $S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$. When $r>1$, $r^n$ grows without bound, so the partial sums have no finite limit. When $0<r<1$, $r^n\to0$ without changing sign, so the partial sums approach $\frac{a}{1-r}$ monotonically. When $-1<r<0$, $r^n$ alternates in sign and approaches 0, so the partial sums alternate about $\frac{a}{1-r}$ with decreasing deviations. When $r<-1$, $r^n$ alternates in sign with increasing magnitude, so the partial sums have no finite limit.

inlines.text: A geometric series has a limiting sum when

answer.worked: When $|r|<1$, $r^n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, giving the finite limiting sum $S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}$.

inlines.text: Let’s confirm this by analysing the limit of the sum:

answer.short: No limiting sum exists for a non-zero first term.
answer.worked: For $r>1$, $r^n$ grows without bound. For $r<-1$, $r^n$ alternates in sign with increasing magnitude. Thus $\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ has no finite limit for $a\ne0$, so $S_\infty$ does not exist.

content.prompt: Find the condition for each GP to have a limiting sum, then find that limiting sum.

answer.worked:
$r=x^2-1$. For a limiting sum, $|r|<1$.
$$\begin{aligned}-1&<x^2-1<1\\0&<x^2<2\end{aligned}$$
Hence $-\sqrt{2}<x<\sqrt{2}$ and $x\ne0$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\frac{a}{1-r}\\S_\infty&=\frac{1}{1-(x^2-1)}\\S_\infty&=\frac{1}{2-x^2}\end{aligned}$$

$r=\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}$. For a limiting sum,
$$\left|\frac{1}{1+x^2}\right|<1.$$
Since $1+x^2\ge1$, this holds exactly when $x\ne0$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\frac{a}{1-r}\\S_\infty&=\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{1+x^2}}\\S_\infty&=\frac{1}{\frac{1+x^2-1}{1+x^2}}\\S_\infty&=\frac{1}{\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}}\\S_\infty&=\frac{1+x^2}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}S_n&=\frac{4(1-3^n)}{1-3}\\S_n&=2(3^n-1).\end{aligned}$$

Thus $-2$ describes the extended formula in the negative direction; it is not the sum of $4+12+36+\cdots$.

$$\begin{align*}S_n&=\frac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]\\735&=\frac{n}{2}[2(15)+(n-1)2]\\735&=\frac{n}{2}[30+2n-2]\\735&=n^2+14n\\0&=n^2+14n-735\end{align*}$$

Using the quadratic formula,

$$\begin{align*}n&=\frac{-14\pm\sqrt{14^2-4(1)(-735)}}{2(1)}\\n&=21\text{ or }-35\end{align*}$$

Since $n>0$, there are $21$ pieces.

$$\begin{align*}a_{21}&=15+(21-1)2\\a_{21}&=55\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

The longest piece of track is $55\text{ cm}$.

answer.short: Kim earns $\$46{,}539.85$ and Alex earns $\$46{,}500$ in the 10th year, so Kim's annual salary is higher.
answer.worked:
Let $K_n$ and $A_n$ be Kim's and Alex's annual salaries in year $n$, respectively.

For Kim, $a=30{,}000$ and $r=1.05$.
$$\begin{align*}K_{10}&=ar^9\\K_{10}&=30{,}000(1.05)^9\\K_{10}&\approx\$46{,}539.85\end{align*}$$
For Alex, $a=33{,}000$ and $d=1500$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{10}&=a+9d\\A_{10}&=33{,}000+9(1500)\\A_{10}&=\$46{,}500\end{align*}$$
Therefore $K_{10}>A_{10}$, as required.

children.label: b
children.prompt: In the first 10 years how much, in total, does Kim earn?

answer.worked:
Kim's annual salaries form a geometric sequence with $a=30{,}000$ and $r=1.05$.
$$\begin{align*}S_n&=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}\\S_{10}&=30{,}000\left(\frac{1.05^{10}-1}{1.05-1}\right)\\S_{10}&\approx\$377{,}336.78\end{align*}$$

children.prompt:

How many years does it take her to save $\$87{,}500$?

answer.worked:
Alex's annual savings are $11{,}000,\ 11{,}500,\ 12{,}000,\ldots$ dollars, an arithmetic sequence with $a=11{,}000$ and $d=500$.

Find $n$ such that $S_n=87{,}500$.
$$\begin{align*}S_n&=\frac n2[2a+(n-1)d]\\87{,}500&=\frac n2[22{,}000+(n-1)500]\\87{,}500&=\frac n2[21{,}500+500n]\\250n^2+10{,}750n-87{,}500&=0\\n^2+43n-350&=0\\(n-7)(n+50)&=0\\n&=7\quad\text{or}\quad n=-50\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Suppose the geometric series $x+x^2+x^3+\cdots$ has a limiting sum.

By considering the graph $y=-1-\dfrac{1}{x-1}$, or otherwise, find the range of possible values of $S_\infty$.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 30, supplied graph below the instruction
spec.description: Editable equation-driven graph with both branches, arrowed axes, dashed asymptotes and the labelled point. No numeric axis ticks or grid are present in the source.
spec.mathematics: y=-1-1/(x-1); vertical asymptote x=1; horizontal asymptote y=-1; point (-1,-1/2); the left branch passes through the origin.
spec.answerVisibility: The complete supplied graph remains visible. The convergence interval and requested range are not marked.

answer.worked:
Here $a=x$ and $r=x$. The limiting sum exists when $|x|<1$, so $-1<x<1$.

$$\begin{align*}
S_\infty&=\frac{a}{1-r}\\
S_\infty&=\frac{x}{1-x}\\
S_\infty&=\frac{-x}{x-1}\\
S_\infty&=\frac{-x+(x-1)-(x-1)}{x-1}\\
S_\infty&=\frac{-x+x-1}{x-1}-\frac{x-1}{x-1}\\
S_\infty&=-\frac{1}{x-1}-1.
\end{align*}$$
This is the function in the supplied graph. On $-1<x<1$, its values increase from the excluded lower bound $-\frac12$ without bound. Hence $S_\infty>-\frac12$.

content.prompt: Pat and Chandra are playing a game. They take turns throwing two dice. The game is won by the first player to throw a double six. Pat starts the game.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the probability that Pat wins the game on the first throw.

answer.worked:
Let $W$ denote throwing a double six.

$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Pat wins on his first throw})&=P(W)\\P(W)&=P(\text{Pat throws two sixes})\\P(W)&=\frac16\times\frac16\\P(W)&=\frac1{36}\end{aligned}$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the probability that Pat wins the game on his first or second throw? Give your answer exactly and to 3 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Let $W$ denote throwing a double six and $L$ denote failing to throw a double six, so $P(L)=\frac{35}{36}$. For Pat to win on his second throw, both Pat and Chandra must first fail.

$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Pat wins on his first or second throw})&=P(W)+P(LLW)\\P(\text{Pat wins on his first or second throw})&=\frac1{36}+\frac{35}{36}\times\frac{35}{36}\times\frac1{36}\\P(\text{Pat wins on his first or second throw})&=\frac{2521}{46656}\\P(\text{Pat wins on his first or second throw})&\approx0.054\quad\text{(to 3 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the probability that Pat eventually wins the game.

answer.worked:
Let $W$ denote throwing a double six and $L$ denote failing to throw a double six.

$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Pat eventually wins})&=P(W)+P(LLW)+P(LLLLW)+\cdots\\P(\text{Pat eventually wins})&=\frac1{36}+\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^2\frac1{36}+\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^2\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^2\frac1{36}+\cdots\end{aligned}$

This is a geometric series with $a=\frac1{36}$ and $r=\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^2=\frac{1225}{1296}$. Since $|r|<1$, its limiting sum exists.

$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\frac{a}{1-r}\\S_\infty&=\frac{\frac1{36}}{1-\frac{1225}{1296}}\\S_\infty&=\frac{36}{71}\end{aligned}$

entries.description: Geometric Sequences
A geometric sequence, also called a geometric progression or exponential sequence, is a sequence where there is a common ratio between each pair of consecutive terms.

The common ratio (r) is the same value that you multiply each term to get the next term. It can be:
• Greater than one (sequence increases, also called exponential growth)
• Between zero and one (sequence decreases, also called exponential decay)
• Negative (sequence alternates between positive and negative terms)

We check whether a sequence is geometric by finding the ratio between consecutive terms and seeing if they are constant.
\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}} = r
